slides.title: Trustworthy experiments
slides.text: Today Trustworthy experiments Session 1 · Assignment, exposure and triggering Who was randomised, who saw the change, and why the triggered effect is the one to estimate Session 2 · Sample ratio mismatch and A/A tests A split that is not what was planned voids the result; A/A tests show the false-win rate the analysis really has Session 3 · Metrics for AI features A primary metric that measures the goal, and guardrails for what an AI feature adds: latency, cost and harm Session 4 · Power for heavy-tailed metrics Sample size from the formula and from simulation on the real distribution, for the population that is triggered

slides.title: One notebook proves your machine is ready
slides.text: Before the first lab One notebook proves your machine is ready uv sync uv run jupyter lab # then run 00_setup_check.ipynb In Colab, open the notebook from the course page: its first cell clones the repository and installs the libraries. Nothing to download : no model, no dataset. The Sufrah data is generated on your machine with fixed seeds. No key : no lab calls a hosted model; the chat-assistant test of Day 4 is analysed from its logs. Quick mode : SUFRAH_QUICK=1 uses 30,000 customers in place of 200,000. The slides quote full mode.

slides.title: Sufrah tests everything, and now it tests AI features
slides.text: The case study Sufrah tests everything, and now it tests AI features The marketplace A fictional food-delivery app in six Saudi cities: 200,000 active customers, restaurants, and couriers shared by everyone. Two AI features AI-ranked search (test T-101) and Luqma, an in-app chat assistant (T-401). Each adds latency, cost and new ways to harm. The people Rawan Al-Mubarak chairs the review board. Yazeed Al-Hamdan owns search. Joud Al-Fahad runs couriers. Waleed Al-Sharif protects data. You are Ruba Kamal, the analyst. All data is synthetic, generated with fixed seeds: about two million orders over 28 pre-period and 28 test days.

slides.title: Assignment, exposure and triggering
slides.text: Session 1 Assignment, exposure and triggering Separate assignment, exposure and the trigger condition in an event log Compute a triggered effect and the diluted overall effect from it Explain why counterfactual logging keeps the control group comparable 01

slides.title: Every test log records three different events
slides.text: Assignment is not exposure Every test log records three different events 1 · Eligible Active in the last 90 days: all 200,000 customers → 2 · Assigned Day 0: a variant for each customer, 50/50 → 3 · Exposed At the first search: the only moment the ranking can matter Triggering. Analyse the customers whose exposure condition held, in both arms. The others can only add noise.

slides.title: Log the trigger in control, where nothing visible happens
slides.text: The control group must be triggered too Log the trigger in control, where nothing visible happens Wrong Triggered treatment customers compared with all control customers. The groups differ in who they are: searchers order more. Right Control logs "would have seen the AI ranking" at the same moment. Both arms are cut by the same rule, so randomisation still holds inside the cut. The trigger must not depend on the treatment. A search happens before the ranking is shown, so the rule is safe. "Clicked a result" would not be.

slides.title: Exposure is one left join and a minimum
slides.text: Lab 1.1, step 2 Exposure is one left join and a minimum select a.customer_id, a.variant, f.exposed_day from assignments a left join (select customer_id, min(day) as exposed_day from searches where day >= 0 group by customer_id) f on f.customer_id = a.customer_id Left join : a customer who never searched stays, with a NULL exposure day. The same pattern counts orders per customer: coalesce(o.orders, 0) keeps the customers who did not order.

slides.title: The triggered lift is nearly twice the diluted one
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.1, full mode The triggered lift is nearly twice the diluted one Population Customers Orders per customer, difference 95% interval Relative All assigned (diluted) 200,000 +0.104 +0.049 to +0.159 +2.0% Triggered 85,080 +0.253 +0.163 to +0.343 +3.9% Dilution. Overall difference ≈ triggered difference × trigger rate: 0.253 × 0.425 = 0.108, against 0.104 measured.

slides.title: Untriggered customers add variance and no signal
slides.text: Why dilution costs power Untriggered customers add variance and no signal The effect shrinks by the trigger rate, here 0.425. The noise does not shrink: 57% of the customers still vary. Dividing the effect by 0.425 multiplies the customers needed by 1 / 0.425² ≈ 5.5; the assigned population is only 1 / 0.425 ≈ 2.4 times the triggered one. 5.5 vs 3.7 standard errors from zero: triggered against diluted (Lab 1.1)

slides.title: Which comparison estimates the effect of AI ranking?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which comparison estimates the effect of AI ranking? T-101 assigned 200,000 customers; 85,080 searched. You want the effect of the new ranking on the people it can reach. Which comparison do you report? Treatment customers who searched against all control customers Customers who searched in treatment against customers who searched in control All treatment customers against all control customers, because it uses more data Each searcher's orders before and after the first search

slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min Triggered and diluted effects in SQL Trace assignment and exposure in SQL and compare the triggered effect with the diluted overall effect, on the event stream of the AI-ranked search test. slides.title: Sample ratio mismatch and A/A tests
slides.text: Session 2 Sample ratio mismatch and A/A tests Test a split against its plan with a chi-square test Locate the cause of a mismatch by segment Measure a false-positive rate with A/A reshuffles of real data 02

slides.title: A split that differs from its plan voids the result
slides.text: The first check on every test A split that differs from its plan voids the result Planned 50/50; observed 50,221 control and 49,028 treatment in T-203. A chi-square test against the plan: p = 0.00015. The users who went missing were not missing at random, so the remaining arms are no longer comparable. 49.4% treatment share in T-203: small to the eye, decisive to the test Never read the metrics of a test that fails this check. Find the cause first.

slides.title: Most mismatches come from what happens after assignment
slides.text: Where mismatches come from Most mismatches come from what happens after assignment Lost The treatment crashes or loads slower on one build, so its users never log an exposure. Filtered A bot filter or a data-quality rule removes more users from one arm. Redirected A treatment that redirects or reloads assigns some users twice or not at all. Diagnose by splitting the counts by every dimension that could lose users unevenly: platform, build, day, browser.

slides.title: One Android build loses one treatment user in seven
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 3 One Android build loses one treatment user in seven iOS 17.2 50.3% iOS 17.3 50.1% Android 7.3 50.6% Android 7.4 46.4% Web 49.3% Treatment share of T-203 users by app build, 14 days.

slides.title: Reshuffle real data to measure the false-win rate you really have
slides.text: A/A tests Reshuffle real data to measure the false-win rate you really have Take 28 days of pre-period revenue per customer. Split the customers at random into two halves. Run the analysis you plan to use. Record p. Repeat 500 times. Count p below 0.05. 5.8% false wins over 500 reshuffles (expected 5% ± 1.9) The customer-level Welch test is calibrated on Sufrah's heavy-tailed revenue.

slides.title: A new feature can win because it is new
slides.text: A trust problem in time A new feature can win because it is new Novelty : customers try the change because it is different; the lift fades. Primacy : customers used to the old version resist; the lift grows. Check the effect by week since first exposure, not only in total. Day 4 Luqma, the chat assistant, lifts orders by 5.8% in week one and by nothing measurable in week four. Lab 4.1 measures it.

slides.title: The result looks good, the split does not
slides.text: Checkpoint The result looks good, the split does not A 50/50 test shows +3% orders with p = 0.002. Its sample ratio check gives p = 0.0004: the treatment arm has 1.2% fewer users than planned. What do you do? Report the lift: the arms are large and the gap is only 1.2% Reweight the treatment arm up to 50% and report the adjusted lift Report no result, find where users are lost, fix it and rerun Correct both p-values for multiple testing and report what survives

slides.title: Sample ratio and A/A checks
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min Sample ratio and A/A checks Run A/A and sample ratio checks on three tests and name the faulty one, then find the segment that causes the mismatch. D1_2_srm_aa_checks.ipynb Users per arm for three tests 3 min A chi-square sample ratio test for each 5 min Find the platform and build that lose users 6 min A/A: 500 reshuffles of the pre-period, the false-win rate 7 min Name the faulty test and its cause in one line 4 min ✱ Stretch: Run the A/A at the order level and explain the higher rate

slides.title: Metrics for AI features
slides.text: Session 3 Metrics for AI features Choose a primary metric that the change can move and that matters to the decision Set latency, cost and harm guardrails with thresholds from baseline data Decide which event data a test may use under purpose limitation and data classification 03

slides.title: One primary metric decides; guardrails can only veto
slides.text: Metric roles One primary metric decides; guardrails can only veto Role Question it answers T-101 example Primary Did the change do what it is for? Orders per triggered customer, 28 days Guardrail Did it break something we will not trade? Search latency, model cost, complaints Diagnostic Why did it move? Clicks on the first result, searches per session A guardrail is not a second primary. A guardrail that "improved" does not rescue a primary that did not move.

slides.title: A model call adds latency, cost and new harms
slides.text: What an AI feature adds A model call adds latency, cost and new harms Latency Every search waits for the model. Measure the tail: p95, not the mean. Cost A price per call, paid on every search, forever. Measure per 1,000 searches. Harm Wrong or unavailable items ranked first, unsafe answers, unfair exposure. Measure complaints and flags. The SDAIA Generative AI Guidelines ask that the risks of a generative feature be assessed and monitored; a harm guardrail is how a test does it.

slides.title: The ramp shows latency and cost at once, not the effect
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 1: the 7-day ramp The ramp shows latency and cost at once, not the effect p50 latency p95 latency Cost per 1,000 searches Keyword ranking 379 ms 676 ms SAR 0.2 AI ranking 543 ms 1,095 ms SAR 5.8 5% of searches on the AI ranking for seven days: about 6,000 searches. Too few to see a 2% change in orders; plenty to see a 400 ms tail.

slides.title: A guardrail is a metric, a direction and a number, written before the test
slides.text: Writing a guardrail A guardrail is a metric, a direction and a number, written before the test {"metric": "search latency p95 (ms), treatment minus control", "kind": "latency", "direction": "at most", "threshold": 300}, {"metric": "inference cost per 1,000 searches (SAR)", "kind": "cost", "direction": "at most", "threshold": 8.0}, {"metric": "complaints per 1,000 orders, upper 95% bound of the difference", "kind": "harm", "direction": "at most", "threshold": 1.0, "harm": true} Harm guardrails use the interval. The upper bound must stay under the line: "no evidence of harm" is not enough.

slides.title: A test may read only the data its purpose needs
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 4 A test may read only the data its purpose needs The Personal Data Protection Law lets a controller process personal data for the purposes it was collected for, and asks that it be limited to the minimum necessary. The NDMO Data Classification Policy has four levels: Top Secret, Secret, Restricted, Public. The level sets how data is protected, not whether this use is allowed. Field Use in T-101? complaint category yes complaint text no: the category suffices exact delivery coordinates no: city suffices allergy profile no: health data

slides.title: The primary wins, a guardrail fails
slides.text: Checkpoint The primary wins, a guardrail fails The AI ranking lifts orders by 3.9% (interval well above zero). Its p95 latency is 420 ms worse; the pre-registered limit was 300 ms. What does the spec say? Not a launch as is: the latency guardrail fails, so the decision rule applies Launch: a 3.9% lift is worth more than 120 ms Raise the latency limit to 450 ms and launch Report latency as a side note to the primary result

slides.title: A metric spec for AI-ranked search
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min A metric spec for AI-ranked search Define a primary metric and latency, cost and harm guardrails for the AI-ranked search test from its ramp data, and decide which fields the analysis may use. D1_3_ai_search_metrics.ipynb Baselines from the ramp: latency, cost, conversion, complaints 6 min The primary metric and its unit 4 min Three guardrails with thresholds and directions 6 min The data inventory: which fields the test may use 6 min Save the metric spec 3 min ✱ Stretch: Add a guardrail that protects small restaurants and say how you would measure it

slides.title: Power for heavy-tailed metrics
slides.text: Session 4 Power for heavy-tailed metrics Compute a sample size with the two-sample formula Estimate power by simulation from historical data Explain when the formula and the simulation disagree for a heavy-tailed metric 04

slides.title: Sample size grows with the variance and with one over the effect squared
slides.text: From the pre-work Sample size grows with the variance and with one over the effect squared n_per_arm = 2 * (z_0.975 + z_0.80)**2 * sd**2 / delta**2 = 2 * 7.85 * sd**2 / delta**2 Halve the effect: four times the customers. Halve the standard deviation: a quarter of them. Day 2 is about the second line.

slides.title: Revenue per customer has a long tail of group orders
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 1 Revenue per customer has a long tail of group orders 511 mean SAR, 28 days, customers who search 295 median SAR 9.4% of revenue from the top 1% of customers Standard deviation 747 SAR, largest customer 31,104 SAR: catering and group orders, about one order in a hundred.

slides.title: Simulate the test you will run on the data you have
slides.text: Power by simulation Simulate the test you will run on the data you have for _ in range(sims): c = rng.choice(values, n) # control arm from history t = rng.choice(values, n) * (1 + lift) # treatment arm, lifted hits += ttest_ind(t, c, equal_var=False).pvalue < 0.05 power = hits / sims Keeps the real distribution, tail included. Works for any analysis: capping, triggering, a sequential plan, a ratio metric.

slides.title: At 84,000 per arm the formula and the simulation agree
slides.text: Lab 1.4, full mode, 400 simulations At 84,000 per arm the formula and the simulation agree Customers per arm Simulated power Formula 20,924 0.31 0.29 41,849 0.57 0.51 83,699 0.77 0.80 104,623 0.85 0.88 What the formula hides. Its standard deviation came from one sample. A sample that missed a few giant orders gives a sigma, and a size, that are too small.

slides.title: Revenue needs twice the traffic of orders for the same 2% lift
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 5 Revenue needs twice the traffic of orders for the same 2% lift Revenue per customer 83,699 per arm, about 55 days Orders per customer 41,480 per arm, about 27 days So T-101 runs 28 days on orders per triggered customer. Revenue becomes a guardrail with a one-sided limit.

slides.title: How many customers for a smaller effect?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many customers for a smaller effect? A test needs 41,000 customers per arm to detect a 2% lift in orders with 80% power. The product manager now wants to detect 1%. Roughly how many per arm? 82,000 58,000 20,500 164,000

slides.title: Power by simulation for the search test
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Power by simulation for the search test Size the search test by simulation on revenue per user and compare with the textbook formula, for triggered customers. D1_4_power_heavy_tails.ipynb Revenue per triggered customer: mean, spread, tail 4 min The formula: customers per arm for a 2% lift 5 min Power by simulation at that size 7 min A power curve and the size for 80% power 5 min Weeks of traffic needed, and the same for orders per customer 4 min ✱ Stretch: Repeat with a 1% lift and say whether the test is worth running

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 Three things to keep Trigger, in both arms Analyse who could be affected, with the same rule in control. Check the split first A sample ratio mismatch voids the test; find the cause before any metric. Write the limits first A primary, guardrails with numbers, and a size from simulation, all before the test.

slides.text: Day 2 Next: the same test, a narrower interval Capping the tail, and what it changes in the estimate Pre-period data that removes most of the noise Intervals for ratio metrics that respect the customer

slides.title: Precision
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Online Experiments and A/B Testing Precision Day 2: The same test, a narrower interval: capping, pre-period data, ratio metrics and strata Data Science Track4 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-302

slides.title: Precision
slides.text: Today Precision Session 1 · Variance and heavy tails Group orders make revenue noisy; capping cuts the variance and changes what is estimated Session 2 · Regression adjustment Pre-period behaviour predicts test behaviour; removing what it predicts narrows the interval Session 3 · Ratio metrics Orders per session is a ratio of two sums per customer; its interval must respect the randomisation unit Session 4 · Stratification Cities differ; using that in design or analysis removes between-city noise, sometimes by little

slides.title: Which check comes first?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which check comes first? Ruba receives the results of a 28-day test with a 4% lift on the primary metric, all guardrails green. Which check does she run before reading any of it? Regression adjustment, to narrow the interval A false discovery correction over the segments The sample ratio check on the assignment counts A power calculation for the observed effect

slides.title: Variance and heavy tails
slides.text: Session 1 Variance and heavy tails Measure how a few large orders drive the variance of revenue per customer Cap a metric at a percentile of the pooled data Report the bias and the variance a cap trades 01

slides.title: One customer in a hundred carries half the variance of revenue
slides.text: Lab 2.1, step 1 One customer in a hundred carries half the variance of revenue 753 SAR, standard deviation of revenue per triggered customer 536 SAR, the same without the top 1% of customers 49% of the variance from that top 1% 85,080 triggered customers, 561,609 test-period orders. About one order in a hundred is a group order worth many baskets.

slides.title: Count each order up to a cap set from both arms pooled
slides.text: Capping, also called winsorising Count each order up to a cap set from both arms pooled cap = orders.value.quantile(0.99) # pooled v = orders.value.clip(upper=cap) revenue = v.groupby(orders.customer_id).sum() Cap SAR 99.9th percentile 1,402 99th percentile 337 95th percentile 184 Never set the cap per arm. A cap that depends on the treatment can create a difference on its own.

slides.title: A capped metric estimates a different, smaller effect
slides.text: The price of a cap A capped metric estimates a different, smaller effect The ranking adds orders, some of them group orders. Capped, those orders count for less: the effect on the capped metric is smaller than on revenue. That gap is a bias if the decision is about revenue. Only in synthetic data The generator knows every customer's orders under both arms, so the true effect of each cap is exact. No real test can measure this bias; a simulation can.

slides.title: The 99th-percentile cap gives the smallest total error
slides.text: Lab 2.1, full mode The 99th-percentile cap gives the smallest total error Cap Estimate Standard error True effect Bias against uncapped Root mean square error none 20.13 5.16 17.91 0 5.16 99.9th 19.71 4.34 17.37 -0.54 4.37 99th 19.11 4.02 16.70 -1.21 4.20 95th 17.92 3.72 15.91 -1.99 4.23 SAR per triggered customer over 28 days.

slides.title: Pre-register the cap, report the uncapped result beside it
slides.text: Writing it down Pre-register the cap, report the uncapped result beside it The percentile and the data it comes from: pooled, before the test. What the metric now means: revenue with each order counted up to SAR 337. The uncapped estimate in the appendix, so nobody wonders what was hidden. Capping is not deleting. The large orders stay in the data; they just stop deciding the interval.

slides.title: Where does the cap come from?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where does the cap come from? Ruba wants to cap order value at the 99th percentile for T-101's revenue metric. Which data should set the cap? Order values from both arms pooled, or from history before the test Order values of the control arm only Each arm's own 99th percentile Whichever cap gives the smallest p-value

slides.title: Capping order value
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min Capping order value Measure how capping order value changes variance and bias, using the potential outcomes the generator knows. D2_1_capping.ipynb Where the variance of revenue comes from 5 min Cap at the pooled 99th and 99.9th percentiles 5 min Effect and standard error under each cap 6 min Bias against the true uncapped effect 5 min Choose a cap and write the reason 4 min ✱ Stretch: Cap per customer instead of per order and compare

slides.title: Regression adjustment
slides.text: Session 2 Regression adjustment Estimate the CUPED coefficient from pre-period data Compute adjusted and unadjusted intervals Report the variance reduction as an effective sample-size gain 02

slides.title: Last month's orders predict this month's, whatever the arm
slides.text: The idea Last month's orders predict this month's, whatever the arm 0.85 correlation between orders in the 28 pre-period days and the 28 test days, triggered customers Most of the variance between customers is habit, and habit was there before the test. Remove what the pre-period predicts and the remaining noise is small. The pre-period cannot carry the effect: it ended before assignment.

slides.title: Subtract theta times the centred pre-period metric
slides.text: CUPED Subtract theta times the centred pre-period metric theta = cov(y, x) / var(x) # both arms pooled y_cuped = y - theta * (x - x.mean()) diff_ci(y_cuped, t) Same expected difference: the term has mean zero in each arm. Variance multiplied by 1 - rho²: here 0.27. theta = 0.864 for orders in T-101.

slides.title: The interval halves; the estimate stays compatible
slides.text: Lab 2.2, full mode The interval halves; the estimate stays compatible Orders per triggered customer Difference Standard error 95% interval Unadjusted +0.253 0.046 +0.163 to +0.343 Adjusted (CUPED) +0.226 0.024 +0.179 to +0.273 73% less variance 3.7× the customers an unadjusted test would need for the same precision

slides.title: Regression adjustment gives the same number to four decimals
slides.text: The same thing, as a regression Regression adjustment gives the same number to four decimals d = df.assign(xc=df.orders_pre - df.orders_pre.mean()) fit = smf.ols("orders ~ treat + xc", data=d).fit(cov_type="HC2") fit.params["treat"], fit.bse["treat"] # 0.2261, 0.0241 The regression form extends to several covariates: pre-period orders, revenue, city. Use robust standard errors; centre the covariate so the treatment coefficient is the average effect.

slides.title: Report the gain as customers: it is what the business buys
slides.text: Reporting the saving Report the gain as customers: it is what the business buys Orders, 28 pre-period days 3.7× the customers Revenue, 28 pre-period days about 1.5× Gain = 1 / (1 - rho²). Orders: rho = 0.85. Revenue: rho = 0.59, so 1 / (1 - 0.34) ≈ 1.5. For T-101 : a revenue test that needed 55 days on Day 1 needs far fewer with capping and adjustment together.

slides.title: What can go into the adjustment?
slides.text: Checkpoint What can go into the adjustment? Ruba wants a stronger adjustment for T-101 and considers adding one more covariate to the regression. Which one is safe? Number of searches during the test Revenue during the test Day of the first search in the test Revenue in the 28 pre-period days

slides.title: Regression adjustment with 28 pre-period days
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · 25 min Regression adjustment with 28 pre-period days Adjust for pre-period behaviour and report the reduction in interval width and the effective sample-size gain. D2_2_cuped.ipynb The unadjusted effect and interval 4 min Theta from the pooled pre-period 5 min The adjusted effect and interval 6 min The same with a regression 5 min Variance reduction and effective sample size 5 min ✱ Stretch: Use 14 pre-period days, the default of one platform, and compare

slides.title: Ratio metrics
slides.text: Session 3 Ratio metrics Explain why a session-level interval is too narrow when customers are randomised Compute a delta-method interval for a ratio metric Check it with a bootstrap over customers 03

slides.title: Orders per session: the numerator and the denominator both vary
slides.text: Ratio metrics Orders per session: the numerator and the denominator both vary Randomised: customers. Counted: sessions and orders. The metric: all orders over all sessions in the arm, a ratio of two sums. Not the mean of each customer's own rate, which weights a one-session customer like a fifty-session one. 0.2036 vs 0.1964 orders per session, treatment and control: +3.7%

slides.title: Treating sessions as independent makes the interval 2.6 times too narrow
slides.text: The trap Treating sessions as independent makes the interval 2.6 times too narrow Naive, sessions as trials ± 0.0009 Delta method, by customer ± 0.0024 Why it matters. An interval 2.6 times too narrow turns noise into wins: the A/A test of Day 1 would show far more than 5% false wins.

slides.title: Compute the variance of a ratio from customer-level sums
slides.text: The delta method Compute the variance of a ratio from customer-level sums o, s = arm.orders, arm.sessions # one row per customer r = o.mean() / s.mean() c = np.cov(o, s) var_r = (c[0,0] - 2*r*c[0,1] + r**2*c[1,1]) / (n * s.mean()**2) A first-order Taylor expansion of mean(O) / mean(S) around its expectation. Every term is per customer, the unit that was randomised.

slides.title: A bootstrap over customers agrees within 4%
slides.text: The check A bootstrap over customers agrees within 4% Method Standard error 95% interval of the difference Naive, sessions 0.00048 +0.0063 to +0.0081 Delta method 0.00124 +0.0048 to +0.0096 Bootstrap, 1,000 resamples of customers 0.00120 +0.0048 to +0.0095 Poisson bootstrap: each customer gets a weight from Poisson(1), all their sessions and orders with it.

slides.title: Which interval is right for clicks per view?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which interval is right for clicks per view? A test randomises customers and reports clicks per page view: 1.9 million views, 80,000 customers. Which standard error should the analysis use? The binomial standard error over 1.9 million views A delta-method standard error over the 80,000 customers The standard error of the mean of each customer's click rate A bootstrap that resamples page views

slides.title: Orders per session: delta method and bootstrap
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · 25 min Orders per session: delta method and bootstrap Compute a delta-method interval for orders per session and check it by a bootstrap over customers. D2_3_delta_method.ipynb Orders per session in each arm 3 min The naive interval, sessions as independent 5 min The delta-method interval 7 min A bootstrap over customers 6 min Two agreeing intervals and why the naive one is narrow 4 min ✱ Stretch: Compute the interval for the relative difference

slides.title: Stratification
slides.text: Session 4 Stratification Distinguish stratified assignment from post-stratification Compute a post-stratified estimate and its standard error Judge when strata help and when pre-period data helps more 04

slides.title: Use the strata in the design, or in the analysis
slides.text: Stratification Use the strata in the design, or in the analysis Stratified assignment Randomise 50/50 inside each city. The arms cannot differ in their city mix. Post-stratification Randomise simply, then estimate city by city and weight by each city's share. Both remove the noise that comes from differences between cities. Neither can remove more than the cities explain.

slides.title: Estimate per city, weight by each city's share
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 3 Estimate per city, weight by each city's share g = d.groupby(["city", "treat"]).orders.agg(["mean", "var", "size"]).unstack("treat") w = (g["size"][0] + g["size"][1]) / len(d) est = (w * (g["mean"][1] - g["mean"][0])).sum() se = sqrt((w**2 * (g["var"][1]/g["size"][1] + g["var"][0]/g["size"][0])).sum())

slides.title: Cities differ in their means, and explain 1.2% of the variance
slides.text: Lab 2.4, step 1 Cities differ in their means, and explain 1.2% of the variance Riyadh 7.36 Jeddah 6.90 Dammam 6.39 Makkah 5.87 Madinah 5.63 Abha 5.09 Orders per triggered customer in the test period. The spread inside each city (standard deviations of 5 to 7.4) dwarfs the spread between them.

slides.title: City strata buy almost nothing; pre-period strata buy a lot
slides.text: Lab 2.4, full mode City strata buy almost nothing; pre-period strata buy a lot Estimator, orders per triggered customer Estimate Standard error Simple difference +0.253 0.046 Post-stratified by city +0.258 0.046 Post-stratified by pre-period deciles +0.227 0.028 CUPED, pre-period orders (Lab 2.2) +0.226 0.024 On a 3,000-customer pilot repeated 1,000 times, city post-stratification cut the variance by 1.3%.

slides.title: When does stratifying by city pay off?
slides.text: Checkpoint When does stratifying by city pay off? Sufrah plans a 2,000-customer pilot in two cities whose customers order at very different rates. slides.title: Group sequential designs
slides.text: Session 1 Group sequential designs Measure the false-positive rate of daily peeking by simulation Compute boundaries from an alpha-spending function Report the false-positive rate, power and expected stopping day of a group sequential test 01

slides.title: Stopping at the first p below 0.05 gives 28% false wins
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 1 Stopping at the first p below 0.05 gives 28% false wins 28.1% of 4,000 simulated tests with no effect cross 1.96 on at least one of 28 daily looks Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line. The daily z values are correlated, so the rate is not 1 - 0.95²⁸, but it is still far above 5%. The fixed test, one look on day 28: 5.3%.

slides.title: Spend the 5% across the looks, on a schedule fixed in advance
slides.text: The idea Spend the 5% across the looks, on a schedule fixed in advance def obf(t, alpha=0.05): # t: share of the plan z = norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) return 2 - 2 * norm.cdf(z / sqrt(t)) Day Alpha spent 7 0.0001 14 0.0056 21 0.0236 28 0.0500 Almost nothing early, when the data is thin; nearly all at the end.

slides.title: Compute each day's boundary by simulation
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 3 Compute each day's boundary by simulation Simulate 40,000 tests with no effect. At day k, among tests not yet stopped, find the |z| that stops exactly the alpha spent at day k, as a share of all tests. Stop those tests; move to day k + 1. Day 7 3.80 Day 14 2.91 Day 21 2.44 Day 28 2.14

slides.title: A group sequential plan is a contract written before day 1
slides.text: What the pre-registration fixes A group sequential plan is a contract written before day 1 The looks How many and when, or the information fractions. The spending O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock or another function, with alpha. The maximum The longest the test may run: 28 days for T-101. Guardrails can stop a test too. A harm guardrail is usually monitored with its own, looser boundary: stopping for harm should be easy.

slides.title: Always-valid tests
slides.text: Session 2 Always-valid tests Compute a mixture sequential probability ratio statistic Measure its false-positive rate under daily monitoring Compare stopping times and power with the group sequential test 02

slides.title: An always-valid test lets you look and stop at any time
slides.text: The other family An always-valid test lets you look and stop at any time No plan of looks, no maximum duration. Its statistic is a likelihood ratio averaged over possible effects; under no effect it never drifts upward on average. So the chance it ever reaches 1 / alpha is at most alpha. Names you will meet mixture SPRT (mSPRT), confidence sequences, anytime-valid inference.

slides.title: The mSPRT statistic needs the estimate, its variance and a width
slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 1 The mSPRT statistic needs the estimate, its variance and a width v = se**2 lam = sqrt(v / (v + tau**2)) * exp(tau**2 * est**2 / (2 * v * (v + tau**2))) stop = lam >= 1 / alpha # 20 for alpha = 0.05 tau , the mixture width, says which effects the test is tuned to: here 0.08 orders, the effect we hope for. Platforms expose it as a tuning parameter; GrowthBook's default is 5,000 observations.

slides.title: Always valid, and far less powerful on a 28-day test
slides.text: Lab 3.2, full mode Always valid, and far less powerful on a 28-day test Design, daily looks False-positive rate Power Mean stopping day Group sequential (O'Brien-Fleming) 0.052 0.759 21.1 mSPRT, tau = 0.08 0.014 0.459 23.1 mSPRT, tau = 0.04 0.004 0.333 25.5 mSPRT, tau = 0.32 0.018 0.378 23.3 The always-valid test spends far less than its 5%: it is built to stay valid beyond day 28 too.

slides.title: Choose by what you can promise in advance
slides.text: Choosing Choose by what you can promise in advance If Use The maximum duration and the looks can be fixed Group sequential: more power for that plan People will look whenever they like, and stop whenever Always valid: the guarantee survives any behaviour One look at the end is enough The fixed test: the most power of all For the capstone. The sequential plan names its family and gives the reason in one line.

slides.title: Which design for a test nobody can stop people watching?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which design for a test nobody can stop people watching? The Luqma team will check results on a public dashboard several times a day and may stop at any moment. The test has no fixed end date. Which design keeps the false-win rate at 5%? A fixed test at alpha = 0.01 A group sequential test with daily looks A Bonferroni correction over the expected number of looks An always-valid test such as mSPRT

slides.title: In a marketplace, one customer's treatment changes another's outcome
slides.text: Interference In a marketplace, one customer's treatment changes another's outcome Treated order Goes to the next free courier first → Same couriers Busy with treated orders → Control order Waits longer than it would without the test No interference is an assumption. A randomised comparison is unbiased only if a unit's outcome depends on its own treatment alone.

slides.title: Cluster and switchback designs
slides.text: Session 4 Cluster and switchback designs Design a city-by-hour switchback Estimate its effect with city and hour adjustments Simulate its power and the bias from carryover 04

slides.title: Randomise what shares the couriers: the city-hour
slides.text: The fix Randomise what shares the couriers: the city-hour Cluster design Whole cities on the new rule. Six units: hopeless power. Switchback Each city switches between rules hour by hour, at random: 6 cities × 14 hours × 14 days = 1,176 blocks. Inside a block every order has the same rule, so nobody jumps a queue of the other arm.

slides.title: One random schedule: Riyadh, day 1
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 1 One random schedule: Riyadh, day 1 Hours 1 to 3 new rule Hours 4 to 6 old rule Hours 7 to 9 new rule Hour 10 old rule Hour 11 new rule Hours 12 to 14 old rule Each operating hour of each city and day is assigned by a coin flip; runs of the same rule happen by chance. Each city has its own schedule.

slides.title: Estimate with city and hour fixed effects, block as the unit
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 2 Estimate with city and hour fixed effects, block as the unit fit = smf.ols("delivery_min ~ treat + C(city) + C(hour)", data=blocks).fit(cov_type="HC1") fit.params["treat"], fit.bse["treat"] # one run: -1.19, se 0.30 One row per city-hour block, not per order: the block was randomised. Each block counts once; weight by orders when the decision is about orders.

slides.title: Seven days give 95% power; the false-win rate stays near 5%
slides.text: Lab 3.4, full mode, 200 runs each Seven days give 95% power; the false-win rate stays near 5% Days Mean estimate (min) Spread Power False wins, no effect 3 -1.42 0.51 0.80 0.050 7 -1.53 0.41 0.95 0.050 14 -1.51 0.30 1.00 0.035

slides.title: Carryover between hours is small in this simulator, so measure it
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 4 Carryover between hours is small in this simulator, so measure it Unfinished deliveries spill into the next hour, whichever rule it has. Measured: switchback with carryover -1.51 minutes, without -1.49. In a real city the spill can be larger: test two-hour blocks, or drop the first hour after each switch. An honest finding. The design choice here is the weighting, not the block length. Your marketplace may differ: simulate yours.

slides.title: What is the unit of analysis in a switchback?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is the unit of analysis in a switchback? Joud's switchback randomised 1,176 city-hour blocks; they contain about 83,000 orders. Ruba computes the standard error from the 83,000 orders as independent rows. What is wrong? The block was randomised, so the standard error must be computed over blocks The estimate is biased by interference Nothing: more rows give a more precise estimate The first hour after each switch must always be dropped

Cost Every call is paid for; cost per conversation is a metric with a limit. Harm A fluent answer can be wrong: an ingredient that is not there, an allergen missed. National reference. slides.title: T-401: Luqma replaces the help menu for half of Sufrah's customers
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · the case T-401: Luqma replaces the help menu for half of Sufrah's customers 60,203 customers with Luqma, 59,797 with the old help menu, four weeks. Primary: orders per customer over the four weeks. Guardrails: p95 response time at most 5 s, cost per conversation at most 0.12 SAR, complaints at most +1.0 per 1,000 orders. Harm guardrail: wrong ingredient or allergen complaints at most +0.3 per 1,000 orders, judged on the upper bound. The written rule Stop if the harm guardrail fails. Otherwise launch if the primary interval is above zero and every guardrail holds; iterate if a non-harm guardrail fails.

slides.title: Twenty cuisine segments, four of them "significant"
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · the case Twenty cuisine segments, four of them "significant" T-205 added photos to menus. Overall: a small lift. The team cut the result by the cuisine of each customer's favourite restaurant: 20 segments. Below 0.05: Mandi (p = 0.00001), Coffee (0.001), Indian (0.040, a drop), Desserts (0.049). 64% of 20-test analyses with no effect anywhere show at least one p below 0.05; 1.0 false win on average

slides.title: Control the chance of any false win, or the share of false wins you report
slides.text: Two error rates to control Control the chance of any false win, or the share of false wins you report Family-wise error: Bonferroni, Holm The chance of even one false win stays at 5%. Bonferroni tests each p against 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025; Holm steps down from the smallest p and never rejects less. False discovery rate: Benjamini-Hochberg Among the segments you report, the expected share of false ones stays at 5%. Sort the p-values; keep the largest k with p(k) ≤ 0.05 k / 20. On the platforms. GrowthBook's documentation offers Holm-Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for many metrics or many variations.

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How packs are scored The rubric Design and power 25% Analysis 25% Monitoring and guardrails 20% Recommendation 20% Reproducibility 10% Every number reruns. A number the board cannot regenerate from the repository scores as a claim, not a result.

slides.title: Ten minutes: seven to present, three for the board
slides.text: Format Ten minutes: seven to present, three for the board 1 · The change and its risk Who it is for, what could go wrong, the harm guardrail. One slide. 2 · The design Unit, metrics, limits, power, the sequential plan, the rule. 3 · The result and the decision The effect with its interval, the guardrails, launch, iterate or stop. Peer feedback. After each defence, everyone writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.

slides.title: One live change, then two questions
slides.text: What the board asks One live change, then two questions The live change The assessor changes the traffic (for example, halves it) or the pre-period (for example, 14 days in place of 28). The participant reruns the power calculation and says what can still be detected and what they would change. "Your harm rate is lower in treatment. Is that evidence the harm is gone?" "Why this spending function, not a fixed horizon?" "Your raw interval includes zero and the adjusted one does not. Which do you report?" "What would make you stop this test on day 10?"
